extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students and novice academic writers (graduate/advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: A handout and class notes giving composition exercises and concrete editorial guidelines to improve clarity, style, and precision in mathematical and academic writing. Combines practice drills (vocabulary, syntax, scansion, precis, invention, etc.) with copy-editing rules and authoring conventions for math papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphatic positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphatic positions in a sentence are the front and the back; the middle is 'sort of a slum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence placement of emphasis (lead or end) to control emphasis; try writing sentences with varying emphasis to learn the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write nonsense (glued nonsense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a completely unrelated stream of thoughts with the correct glue (connectives like 'thus,' 'therefore,' 'as we can see').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an exercise in cohesion—create coherent transitions among unrelated ideas. Suggested as a playful exercise (Mary-Claire: 'incredibly wonderful'), possibly after a couple of drinks; can be done repeatedly to practice connective usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual labor: copying in many modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy out passages of writing by hand and by different physical modes (pen, pencil, crayon, left hand, right hand, manual typewriter, word-processor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying slows the brain for close reading, reveals patterns, and connects hand movement to thought. Also copy passages you like, dislike, find difficult, easy, written by someone you'd like to imitate, from different eras or conditions. Use copying as exploratory close reading to learn stylistic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorization and recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorize and recite passages to be able to read word by word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recitation and memorization help internalize cadence and phrasing, improving detailed reading and writing sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds: transcribe and read aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe short recordings (radio news, conversation, lecture) and have others read or listen to your writing aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcription trains ear for natural speech; reading your work aloud (and having others do so) reveals cadence and tone problems. Learn to mutter what you're writing as a quick check for cadence/tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper: use revision as tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that writing is 'the most forgiving medium known to man' — 'How do I know what I mean till I see what I say?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ability to revise (marks on paper) to iterate until the meaning is right; don't expect perfect first drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance, voice, and tone — change stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a textbook explanation as a personal letter to different audiences (nephew, spouse, reporter, psychiatrist, anthropologist, police inspector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing rewriting for different audiences trains register control and shows how tone and stance alter content and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take both sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a vigorous, closely reasoned argument for some small household policy, then write a vigorous argument against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercises the ability to see and construct coherent opposing arguments; useful for anticipating objections and tightening reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolize
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe objects/events in exaggerated ways (e.g., describe your dwelling as an unscrupulous realtor would).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration helps reveal definitional and descriptive choices and their effects on reader perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphemize
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe unpleasant facts (medical symptoms, forced resignation) accurately but using euphemistic or prudish diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice controlling register and the social effect of diction; useful for learning how language choices shape tone and implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obfuscate
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a simple passage so that the same ideas seem obscure and difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how syntax and diction can create opacity; useful anti-pattern awareness for clearer writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pontificate
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a straightforward first-person passage to make the author sound pompous and self-important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps recognize and avoid pompous tone; see how small changes inflate perceived authorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacillate (inject doubts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take an argumentative passage and inject doubts, quibbles, and hesitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice weakening arguments deliberately and then reversing the exercise to strengthen them; useful for rhetorical control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen and vitiate paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a weak, flabby paragraph and rewrite to make it vigorous; then take a strong paragraph and weaken it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches concrete techniques for tightening prose and for spotting unnecessary weight or flabbiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change tone (translate sarcasm/factuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite sarcastic pieces as short factual writing (e.g., rewrite a sarcastic letter to an objective petition preamble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice shifting rhetorical stance while preserving factual content; useful to control audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation exercises (expand/contract, rethink, sensualize, Agassiz leaf)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a small daily event and expand to five pages then cut back; describe an object by appearance only or by sounds only; describe by each sense; repeatedly describe a single leaf or flower each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches careful sensory description, focus, and the effects of compression/expansion on meaning and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same as and different from (compare, analogize, differentiate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create similes capturing a point of similarity; invent analogies to explain complex institutions to naive audiences; write short dictionary-like differentiations among similar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy and comparison exercises practice pedagogical clarity and precision in distinguishing related concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention: combine and categorize
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose random dictionary words and force them into sentences; take random nouns and categorize them with an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice generating unexpected connections and classification schemes—helps build inventive habits of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion and verse exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Render prose into formal verse (couplets, villanelle, ballad, sonnet), write new sonnets daily, change meter (tetrameter→pentameter), and respect conventional rhyme and stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing verse trains rhythm, stress, and concision in prose; honor conventional prosody to get full benefit (avoid near-misses). Consult prosody handbooks (e.g., Hollander).

rubrics_metrics.name: Précis: reduction without meaning change
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a passage, count words, and reduce them by given percentages (5%, 25%, 50%) without changing meaning; write abstracts (≤10 sentences) describing an article or book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches compression and structural rethinking when cutting length; at some reduction percentages structural change is unavoidable—do not change meaning, but accept loss of details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly real exercises (flip, replace, crunch, unpack, define, exemplify, explain, instruct, translate, Ben Franklin, push)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of realistic tasks: reorder paragraph sentences (flip); alter pacing (replace); describe object without adjectives/adverbs (crunch); unpack metaphors to prose; write dictionary definitions and compare; give ordered examples of an abstract noun; rewrite instructions for novices; write instructions without naming the object; write jokes; translate from an unfamiliar language with a bilingual dictionary; reconstruct a passage from one- and two-word hints (Ben Franklin); timed continuous sentence writing (push).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises approximate real writing tasks—compression, pacing, technical explanation, pedagogy, translation, constrained writing, and improvisation. Try them and test them (e.g., try instructions on a friend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes / rhetorical figures practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Work through a rhetoric handbook and write an example for every rhetorical figure listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing the exercises (not just thinking) is necessary—producing examples yields deeper understanding than mere reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of 'which' vs 'that'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'which' and 'that' according to prescriptive distinction; avoid unnecessary 'which' where 'that' is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuse often arises under pressure and creates a bad tone (sounds nervous). Keep text editable online and check occurrences; instructors may quiz on correct usage. Fowler gives rule but enforcement varies historically/regionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheadings must not be integral
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should make sense if read omitting subsection titles; subheadings should act like marginal notes rather than integral text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid referring explicitly to the subheading inside the paragraph. Make subsections self-contained so the flow remains if headings are removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms clearly and early
rubrics_metrics.description: Define basic and field-specific terms at the start (especially in fields like graph theory where different authors use terms inconsistently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what background readers share and what they may not know. Be explicit about notation and symbols before using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct; avoid unnecessary definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense multi-part definitions when possible; do not define terms you never use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Less is more.' Shorten intimidating multi-part definitions if parts are unused; avoid noisy verbosity that burdens readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of terminology across coauthors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same names for the same concepts (avoid calling the same thing 'dominators' in one place and 'parents' in another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agree on terms with coauthors early; invent alternate names if needed to avoid symbol clutter; inconsistency confuses readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense accuracy in technical statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose tense appropriately: algorithms 'have' shown (present perfect) rather than 'had' shown when stating timeless facts about algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between timeless facts about algorithms and historical changes about problems; use tense that reflects intended meaning to avoid logical anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation formatting and parenthetical references
rubrics_metrics.description: References should be parenthetical and not interrupt sentence flow (avoid 'Tarjan[Gab83]' glued to preceding word or odd bracket styles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parenthetical citations so sentences read sensibly without them; consider style guides (Chicago Manual of Style) and automation (TeX/BibTeX) to manage references consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage guided by speech pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid too many commas; a rough guide is to place a comma where a speaker would pause for breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify punctuation when commas clutter sentences (example given where punctuation around variable names should be adjusted). Read aloud to judge pausing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous words and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer unambiguous terms (e.g., 'self-loop' instead of 'loop'; avoid ambiguous uses of 'left' or overloaded symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a word has multiple senses in the context (e.g., 'left' as direction vs. past tense), rephrase to avoid ambiguity. If symbols like Hi and Hj will cause confusion, re-name or rephrase ('each Hi is ...') to maintain clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use lemmas/theorems before proving them
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using a lemma or theorem earlier in text than where it is proved, which can confuse readers about logical ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure proofs and statements so that dependencies are clear; ensure readers are not led to suspect circular reasoning (using a result to prove itself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nonbreaking ties to prevent awkward line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ties/nonbreaking spaces (e.g., in TeX) to keep related tokens together (e.g., after 'dominates' or between 'e' and 'is') so line breaks don't distort meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent line breaks that split phrases in ways that interrupt or distort the message; apply ties after prepositions/short tokens where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idiom collisions and confusing terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary when a common idiom clashes with a technical sense of a word in the paper (e.g., 'n vertices have been deleted' alongside complex planes/airplanes causing confusing 'plane').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase to avoid accidental double meanings in a technical context; anticipate domain-specific collisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build sequences of examples that develop
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sequence of examples that build on one another rather than a set of unrelated ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A progressive sequence aids reader comprehension and demonstrates concept development; prefer layered examples in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep text accessible for easy editing checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain copies of your text online/accessible so you can quickly locate and fix recurring errors (e.g., misuse of 'which').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical workflow tip: ease of access facilitates iterative correction and responding to instructor/editor feedback.
